title: What Is Kaomoji? Meaning, Origin and How to Use Them
description: Learn what kaomoji are, where the word comes from, how they differ from emoticons and emoji, and how to use kaomoji in your messages.
lead: Kaomoji (顔文字) are Japanese-style faces made from text characters, like (˶ᵔ ᵕ ᵔ˶) or (ﾉ◕ヮ◕)ﾉ*:･ﾟ✧. This guide explains what they are, where they come from, and how to use them well.

sections.p: The word kaomoji joins two Japanese words: kao, meaning face, and moji, meaning character. So kaomoji means face characters. The faces are drawn with letters, punctuation, and symbols, which is why you can type or paste them anywhere text is allowed.

Kaomoji is the standard spelling, and it is used for both one face and many. English speakers often add an s and write kaomojis, and some people type kamoji by mistake. All three spellings point to the same thing, so you can use whichever feels natural.

Kaomoji grew out of early Japanese online communities and text messaging, where people wanted to show feeling with the characters they already had. Japanese writing offers many extra characters, including katakana, which is why kaomoji can look so rich and detailed.

A typical kaomoji has a pair of eyes, a mouth, and sometimes arms or decorations. Each part is a character. For example, ◕ can be an eye, ᴗ a mouth, and ♡ a heart beside the face. Because most of the feeling sits in the eyes, kaomoji read upright instead of sideways, unlike Western emoticons such as :).

sections.h: Kaomoji symbols: the characters behind the faces
sections.p: Kaomoji symbols come from many parts of Unicode, the standard that defines text characters. You will find katakana such as ヮ and ツ, math and shape symbols like ◕ and ▽, accent marks, and small decorations like ♡ and ✧. Because these are all text, the faces copy and paste like any other word.

sections.h: Kaomoji vs emoticons vs emoji vs ASCII art
list: Emoticons are short text faces like :) that you read sideways.
Kaomoji are Japanese-style text faces that you read upright.
Emoji are small pictures from the Unicode standard, and they look different on each device.
ASCII art uses text to draw bigger pictures, and kaomoji are tiny, one-line versions of it.

sections.p: Some kaomoji became internet classics. You can copy the [shrug emoticon](/kaomoji/shrug.html), the [lenny face](/kaomoji/lenny-face.html), and the [table flip](/kaomoji/table-flip.html) from their own pages, or browse the [meme faces](/kaomoji/meme.html). For sweeter styles, visit [cute kaomoji](/kaomoji/cute.html) and [aesthetic kaomoji](/kaomoji/aesthetic.html).

list: Pick a face that fits the tone of your message.
Use one face at a time so it stays easy to read.
Save your favorites so they are quick to find.
Remember that screen readers may read every symbol aloud, so do not rely on a kaomoji for important meaning.

sections.p: Ready to try them? Browse [happy kaomoji](/kaomoji/happy.html) and [love kaomoji](/kaomoji/love.html), or read how to [copy and paste kaomoji](/how-to-copy-and-paste-kaomoji.html) on your device. To see how the faces are built, read about [kaomoji symbols](/kaomoji-symbols.html), or find out [where to use kaomoji](/kaomoji-for-discord-instagram-tiktok.html).

title: Japanese Emoticons: Kaomoji, ASCII Art and Symbols Explained
description: Understand Japanese emoticons: how kaomoji differ from Western emoticons, smiley faces, ASCII art and symbols, and where to copy them.
lead: Japanese emoticons, called kaomoji, are text faces that you read upright. This guide compares them with Western emoticons, smiley faces, ASCII art, and symbol sets, so you know which one to use.

sections.p: Japanese emoticons are faces made from text characters, such as (^_^) or (ᵔ◡ᵔ). They are called kaomoji in Japanese, and you will also see them described as text faces or cute emoticons. They show feeling mostly through the eyes.

Western emoticons, like :-) and :(, are written sideways and use only a few characters. Japanese emoticons are written upright and often use extra symbols for blush marks, arms, hearts, and sparkles. That makes them more expressive for the same amount of space.

A smiley face can be a text emoticon, a Unicode symbol such as ☺, or an emoji picture. Symbols and emoticons are related, because kaomoji symbols are the building blocks of every face. A heart emoticon, for instance, uses ♡ or ♥ next to a face. If you want a ready-made smile, try the [happy kaomoji](/kaomoji/happy.html) page. Our guide to [kaomoji symbols](/kaomoji-symbols.html) lists the characters and their Unicode names.
ASCII art draws pictures with text, sometimes across many lines. Kaomoji are a small, single-line cousin of ASCII art. They are easier to send in messages and easier to read at a glance.

list: [Cute emoticons](/kaomoji/cute.html) with sparkly eyes and blushing cheeks
[Heart emoticons](/kaomoji/love.html) for hugs, kisses, and love notes
[Star emoticons](/kaomoji/aesthetic.html) and sparkles for a dreamy look

sections.h: Emoticons copy paste: how it works here
sections.p: Emoticons copy and paste is simple here, because every face on this site is ready to copy. Tap it, then paste it into your chat, caption, or bio. For step-by-step instructions on each device, read [how to copy and paste kaomoji](/how-to-copy-and-paste-kaomoji.html).

title: How to Copy and Paste Kaomoji on iPhone, Android, Windows and Mac
description: Step-by-step help for copying and pasting kaomoji on iPhone, Android, Windows and Mac, plus fixes for boxes and broken symbols.
h1: How to copy and paste kaomoji
lead: Copying a kaomoji takes one tap, and pasting works the same way as any other text. Here are the steps for each device, and what to do when a face looks wrong.

sections.h: Kaomoji copy paste: the quick way on this site
sections.p: Find a face, then tap it. It is copied to your clipboard right away, and a small message confirms it. Then paste it where you want it. You can also tap the heart to save the face to your favorites.

After copying, tap and hold in a text box and choose Paste. To use a favorite face often, you can add it as a text replacement in your keyboard settings, so a short word turns into the face. Settings names can change between iOS versions.

After copying, long-press in a text field and tap Paste. Many Android keyboards also keep a clipboard of recent items, and some let you save a shortcut for a face in the personal dictionary. Exact menus depend on your keyboard app.

On a computer, paste with Ctrl+V on Windows or Cmd+V on a Mac. Recent versions of Windows also include a kaomoji tab in the emoji panel, which opens with the Windows key and the period key. On a Mac, you can save a face as a text replacement in keyboard settings.

sections.h: Why a kaomoji shows boxes or looks broken
sections.p: Boxes usually mean your device lacks a font for one of the symbols. Try another face, update your device, or switch to a different keyboard. Some apps also change the look of special marks, so a face may look slightly different from one app to another.

sections.h: Why the shrug loses its arm
sections.p: In apps such as Discord and Slack, a backslash before an underscore can be read as formatting. The shrug then loses its arm. Type a second backslash, or paste the face inside a code block, to fix it. You can find the shrug and other classics on the [shrug emoticons](/kaomoji/shrug.html) page.
Screen readers may read each symbol in a kaomoji out loud, which can sound long. Keep faces short, and put the important meaning in words. This keeps your message clear for everyone.

Browse [cute kaomoji](/kaomoji/cute.html), [happy kaomoji](/kaomoji/happy.html), or the full list on the [homepage](/index.html). To learn more about the faces themselves, read [what is kaomoji](/what-is-kaomoji.html). Wondering which apps work best? See [kaomoji for Discord, Instagram, and TikTok](/kaomoji-for-discord-instagram-tiktok.html).

title: Kaomoji Symbols and Emoticon Characters: Meanings and Unicode
description: A reference of kaomoji symbols and emoticon characters: the eyes, mouths, cheeks, arms and decorations used in text faces, with Unicode names.
lead: Every kaomoji is built from small symbols. This guide lists the most common emoticon symbols used in text faces, with their Unicode code points and official names, so you can see how a face is put together and why it sometimes breaks.

sections.p: Kaomoji symbols are the text characters that make up a kaomoji. They come from many parts of Unicode, the standard that gives every character a code number. Some are letters from other alphabets, like the Greek ω. Others are shapes, katakana, or punctuation. Used together, they draw a face.

sections.h: How a kaomoji is put together
sections.p: Most faces follow the same pattern: an outline made of brackets, a pair of eyes, a mouth, and sometimes cheeks, arms, or decorations. For example, in (づ｡◕‿‿◕｡)づ the づ marks are arms, ｡ marks are cheeks, ◕ marks are eyes, and ‿‿ is the smile. Changing one symbol changes the mood of the whole face.
Eyes carry most of the feeling in a kaomoji, which is why kaomoji read upright instead of sideways.

sections.h: Symbols and emoticons: what is the difference?
sections.p: Symbols are single characters, like ♡ or ✿. Emoticons are faces built from several symbols. People also search for emoticons symbols or emoticon symbols, and both mean the characters used to build text faces. They are the parts, and a kaomoji is the finished face. You can use symbols alone as decoration, or combine them to make your own emoticon. See [aesthetic kaomoji](/kaomoji/aesthetic.html) for examples.

The easiest way is to copy a whole face from this site. If you want to type a symbol yourself, you have a few options. In Microsoft Word on Windows, you can type the code, such as 2661, and press Alt and X to turn it into ♡. On Windows, the emoji panel (Windows key and period) has a kaomoji tab. On a Mac, the Character Viewer in the Edit menu lists symbols you can insert. Many phone keyboards also have a symbols page.

sections.h: Why some kaomoji symbols show as boxes
sections.p: A box means the font on your device does not include that character. Rare symbols, like some Kannada letters or combining marks, are the usual cause. Try another face, switch apps, or update your system. For more help, read [how to copy and paste kaomoji](/how-to-copy-and-paste-kaomoji.html).

title: Kaomoji for Discord, Instagram, TikTok and WhatsApp
description: How to use kaomoji on Discord, Instagram, TikTok, WhatsApp, X and more: where they work, common problems, and tips for bios and display names.
h1: Kaomoji for Discord, Instagram, TikTok and WhatsApp
lead: Kaomoji are plain text, so they work almost everywhere you can type. This guide covers the apps people ask about most, the small problems you may meet, and how to fix them.

sections.p: Kaomoji work in messages, nicknames, and statuses on Discord. The one catch is formatting: Discord reads underscores, asterisks, and backslashes as markdown, which can change a face. The shrug is the classic example, which loses its arm. Type a second backslash, or put the face inside a code block, to keep it whole. See [shrug emoticons](/kaomoji/shrug.html) for more.

You can paste kaomoji into your bio, captions, comments, and messages. Bios have limited space, so short faces work best. Soft, simple styles like [cute kaomoji](/kaomoji/cute.html) and [aesthetic kaomoji](/kaomoji/aesthetic.html) are popular for bios. Check that the face looks right after you save, since the display font can differ from your keyboard.

Kaomoji work in TikTok comments, captions, and your bio. Keep them short in places with tight limits. Happy and cute faces, like [happy kaomoji](/kaomoji/happy.html), are a quick way to add personality to a comment.

WhatsApp uses asterisks and underscores for formatting, so a face that contains them may change. If a face looks wrong, try one without those characters. Greeting and love faces, like [greeting kaomoji](/kaomoji/greetings.html) and [love kaomoji](/kaomoji/love.html), work well in chats.

sections.h: Kaomoji on X, Telegram, Snapchat and YouTube
sections.p: All of these accept plain text, so you can paste kaomoji into posts, replies, chats, and comments. Watch for character limits, because some symbols count as more than one character.

sections.h: Kaomoji in usernames and display names
sections.p: Many apps allow special characters in display names, but rules differ, and some apps strip or block certain symbols. Test the name first, and avoid using a kaomoji in an account name you cannot easily change.

sections.h: Kaomoji in email, documents and notes
sections.p: Kaomoji paste into email, documents, and notes the same way as any text. In formal writing, one face is enough, and many people skip them in work emails.

list: A box appears: try another face or update your system fonts.
A part of the face is missing: the app may be reading a symbol as formatting, so use a code block or another face.
The face looks different: apps use different fonts, so spacing can change a little.
The paste fails: copy again, or paste into a plain text field first.

sections.p: Start with [cute kaomoji](/kaomoji/cute.html), [happy kaomoji](/kaomoji/happy.html), and [love kaomoji](/kaomoji/love.html). For classics, try the [shrug](/kaomoji/shrug.html), [lenny face](/kaomoji/lenny-face.html), and [table flip](/kaomoji/table-flip.html). To learn how the faces are built, read [kaomoji symbols](/kaomoji-symbols.html).
